                                           I.       INTRODUCTION

         The New Mexico Large Customer Group (“NMLCG”) submits this Response Brief

responding to certain issues raised in New Mexico Public Regulation Commission

(“Commission”) Staff’s (“Staff”) and Southwestern Public Service Company’s (“SPS” or

“Company”) Initial Post-Hearing Briefs.1 The NMLCG continues to support the Comprehensive

Stipulation (“Stipulation”),2 and urges the Commission to approve the Stipulation in its entirety.

Below, the NMLCG briefly responds to (1) Staff’s revenue allocation position; and (2) SPS’s

Production Tax Credit (“PTC”) Deferred Tax Asset (“DTA”) return proposal; and (3) and clarifies

a mischaracterization in SPS’s Post-Hearing Brief regarding the Excess Liability Insurance

(“ELI”) regulatory asset.

                                II.      RESPONSE TO STAFF’S BRIEF

         Staff recognizes the Stipulation, compared to Staff’s direct case, produces a more favorable

revenue allocation for residential and small commercial classes when compared at the same

revenue increase.3 But Staff attempts to distract from this fact. It argues the “normalized

comparison” between the Stipulation’s and Staff’s revenue allocations “is a diversion from the

salient point that residential ratepayers are receiving a higher bill increase under the

Stipulation....”4      Staff further challenges the Stipulation’s revenue allocation, asserting

“gradualism and banding...have no influence on whether the underlying revenue requirement itself

is just and reasonable.”5

          While the NMLCG does not dispute Staff’s point that the overall rate increase would be

lower under Staff’s direct case compared to the Stipulation, the Commission should reject Staff’s

flawed analysis and review the Stipulation’s revenue allocation as just and reasonable when

viewed as part of the Stipulation overall. Revenue requirement and revenue allocation are two

distinct ratemaking items that should be reviewed in isolation. Indeed, the Stipulation’s revenue

allocation proposal, coupled with Staff’s revenue requirement, would produce lower residential

and small commercial rate increases compared to Staff’s direct case. Thus, it is unclear why Staff

opposes the Stipulation’s revenue allocation.

         Staff further undermined its own position at hearing, recognizing that settlements require

compromise, “give-and-take,” and movement from original positions.6                            Accordingly, large

consumers, residential advocates, and environmental interests compromised with the Company,

agreeing to a revenue requirement that exceeded the parties’ direct cases. As part of this

compromise, the Stipulation provides residential and small commercial consumers with rate

mitigation and favorable revenue allocations7 and other notable benefits, including a bolstered

Electric Affordability Program.8 Despite Staff’s statements at hearing, it fails to appreciate this

compromise, jeopardizing a Stipulation that furthers Staff’s own affordability objectives.

         In short, all parties representing diverse interests—excluding Staff—urge the Commission

to adopt the Stipulation.9 Staff’s opposition, moreover, is flawed and undermines Staff’s own

 objectives. The Commission should therefore reject Staff’s opposition and, in accordance with

                               III.    RESPONSE TO SPS’S BRIEF

        The NMLCG generally agrees with the Company: the Comprehensive Settlement is in the

public interest, delivers substantial benefits to customers, and should be adopted in its entirety.11

SPS’s PTC DTA carrying charge time limit proposal, however, would undermine these customer

benefits. The Company also mischaracterized the Stipulation regarding the ELI regulatory asset

agreement. The NMLCG addresses these issues in turn below.

        A.      The Company’s PTC DTA carrying charge time limit proposal entitles the
                Company to excessive DTA carrying charges.

        The Hearing Examiners requested that parties propose a “recommended methodology to

ensure that [PTCs] accrued in a [DTA] by SPS do not carry forward for an unreasonable amount

of time.”12 Under the Stipulation, certain PTCs in the DTA earn a return equal to SPS’s long-term

cost of debt.13 Thus, a reasonable PTC carrying charge accrual limitation is necessary to protect

ratepayers from perpetual PTC carrying charges.

        The Company proposes a two-year cap, limiting PTC carrying charges to PTCs generated

within the previous two years.14 SPS relies on Internal Revenue Code (“IRC”) federal transfer

election deadline provisions related to PTC transfers.15 Specifically, to receive credit for a PTC

transfer, the IRC requires the Company to transfer the PTC within 22 months.16 According to SPS,

“strong public policy” favoring settlements).

                                                     3
 this federal PTC transfer limitation demonstrates that PTC carrying charges accrued over two years

are reasonable.

           The Company’s proposal should be rejected for three reasons. First, IRC regulations have

no nexus with New Mexico ratepayer protections set by the Commission. The federal transfer

election deadline does not establish that 22 months is a reasonable period for customers to bear

carrying costs on the associated DTA. Put differently, SPS’s ability to meet minimum federal tax

standards is not a reasonable basis for allowing greater returns at New Mexico ratepayers’ expense.

           Second, the Company’s position results in excessive costs. Indeed, a PTC remaining

outstanding for two years, under the Company’s proposal carrying charges at 5.29% (the long-

term cost of debt) annually, would amount to an unreasonable accumulation of carrying costs. If

the PTC is subsequently transferred, customers may also bear transfer costs of up to 10% of the

nominal value of the PTC. These potential costs further support a limitation based on a reasonable

period for monetization rather than the outer limit for making a transfer election under federal tax

law.

           Third, the Company previously testified that “180 days...is the average estimated time that

SPS expects to sell the PTC after generation.”17 Therefore, the NMLCG’s proposal to cap SPS

earning a carrying charge at 365 days provides a reasonable opportunity to earn carrying charges

while SPS works to sell the PTCs (more than double the average amount of time) while also

capping the length of time carrying charges are earned, protecting customers from SPS accruing

unreasonable carrying charges and providing SPS appropriate incentives to timely monetize the

PTCs for customers’ benefit.




17
     Case No. 24-00270-UT, SPS Ex. 4 (Trammel Sup. Dir.), p. 14:3-8.



                                                         4
          The Commission should therefore impose a 365-day cap on PTC accruals, prohibiting the

Company from earning carrying charges on PTCs more than 365 days after generation. This

represents a compromise, protecting ratepayers from unnecessary PTC carrying charges while

providing the Company with significant flexibility to sell PTCs.

         B.        The Company mischaracterized the Stipulation in regard to the ELI
                   Regulatory Asset.

         In its Brief, SPS responds to Staff’s challenges regarding the Company’s ELI balance,

asserting the Company “updated the deferred ELI balance to $26,233,655” and “[t]he stipulated

cost of service uses that updated amount.”18 The Stipulation, however, did not agree to a specific

ELI balance.19 Rather, it merely authorizes the Company to recover “[a] three-year amortization

of deferred [ELI] premiums approved in Case No. 25-00030-UT.”20 The NMLCG raises this point

to clarify the record.

                                    IV.     CONCLUSION

         The NMLCG respectfully requests that the Commission approve the Stipulation in its

entirety. Additionally, the NMLCG requests that the Commission limit PTC carrying charge

accrual to 365 days after the Company generates the PTC.
